pos: n. (Ann Griffiths, 1776–1805, of Dolwar Fach in Montgomeryshire, Welsh Calvinistic Methodist hymn-writer)
etymology: Hebrew Channah, grace; Welsh Griffiths, son of Gruffudd.
biblical_def: Ann Griffiths was a farmer's daughter of Dolwar Fach, near Llanfihangel-yng-Ngwynfa, who spent her girlhood at dances and fairs and was converted in 1796 under the preaching of a Calvinistic Methodist minister at Llanfyllin. She joined the Methodist society at Pontrobert, walked many miles to the communion at Bala, and gave herself to the study of Scripture with an intensity her neighbours remembered. She married Thomas Griffiths in 1804 and died the next year, aged twenty-nine, a few weeks after the birth and death of her daughter. She never wrote down most of her hymns. She sang them to her maid, Ruth Evans, who memorized them and repeated them to her husband, John Hughes of Pontrobert, who wrote them out; some seventy stanzas survive. They are among the greatest religious poems in the Welsh language: dense with Scripture, centred on the person of Christ as God and man, and filled with wonder at the cross, at the covenant, and at the Mediator who is “the chiefest among ten thousand” (Son 5:10). Her theme is the mystery Paul confessed: “God was manifest in the flesh” (1Ti 3:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hymn as a song or ode in honor of God, and a society in religion as a number of persons united for a religious purpose.
webster_full: HYMN, n. A song or ode in honor of God, or in honor of some deity.
SOCI'ETY, n. A number of persons associated for any temporary or permanent object; an association for mutual profit, pleasure or usefulness.
MEDIA'TOR, n. By way of eminence, Christ is the mediator, the divine intercessor through whom sinners may be reconciled to an offended God.
scriptures: Son 5:10
My beloved is white and ruddy, the chiefest among ten thousand.

And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee.
corruption_summary: A farmhouse hymn-writer whose verses were saved by a servant's memory.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Modern admirers sometimes read Ann Griffiths as a mystic in the medieval manner, a soul lost in contemplation. Her hymns are nothing of the kind. They are theology sung, built from Scripture memorized as the psalmist memorized it, “Thy word have I hid in mine heart” (Psa 119:11), and their wonder rests on doctrine: the two natures of Christ, the covenant of redemption, the substitution of the cross.

The principle to recover is that the richest devotion comes from the plainest doctrinal precision, and that the church's song should be “the word of Christ” dwelling richly (Col 3:16). Her hymns survived because a servant girl carried them in her memory; the church that values them should carry the Scripture they are made of the same way.

Greek musterion (G3466) — a mystery, a revealed secret; 1 Timothy 3:16.

“God was manifest in the flesh” (1Ti 3:16) — her constant wonder.
“Thy word have I hid in mine heart” (Psa 119:11) — how her verses were made and kept.

pos: n. (Thomas Jones, 1756–1820, Welsh Calvinistic Methodist minister, theologian, and biographer of Thomas Charles)
etymology: Aramaic Teoma, a twin; Welsh Jones, son of John; Denbigh, from Welsh Dinbych, little fortress.
biblical_def: Thomas Jones was born at Caerwys in Flintshire, intended for Anglican orders, but joined the Calvinistic Methodists and became, after Thomas Charles, the most learned man in their connexion. He lived successively at Mold, Ruthin, and Denbigh, preaching widely, writing, and translating. In 1811, when the Welsh Methodists finally ordained their own ministers rather than depend on sympathetic Anglican clergy for the sacraments, he was among the men set apart at Bala, and so stood at the moment the revival became a church. Jones wrote theology in Welsh for ordinary readers, defending the doctrines of grace against both the Arminianism of the Wesleyan preachers who entered North Wales and the high Calvinism that would not freely offer Christ to sinners. He also wrote hymns and devotional works and, after Charles's death in 1814, a life of his friend. His balance was Paul's, who held that salvation is “not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16), and who commanded the church to “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a connexion as a religious body united in fellowship, and ordination as the act of conferring holy orders.
webster_full: CONNEC'TION, n. The act of joining or state of being joined; union by relation; a religious body united under one system.
ORDINA'TION, n. The act of conferring holy orders, or of setting apart for the gospel ministry.
ARMIN'IANISM, n. The peculiar doctrines or tenets of the Arminians, who deny the doctrine of predestination and maintain universal redemption.
scriptures: Rom 9:16
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Jer 3:15
And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
corruption_summary: A Welsh Methodist theologian who kept the doctrines of grace between Arminianism and hyper-Calvinism.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The danger Jones answered is perennial in revival movements: that warmth will outrun doctrine, and that the converts of one generation will be claimed by whichever system preaches loudest to the next. A ministry that will last must be the one Jeremiah promised, “pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jer 3:15).

The principle to recover is that the free offer of Christ and the sovereignty of grace are held together in Scripture and must be held together in preaching. A minister must be able “by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9), and Jones did both, on two fronts at once.
roots_summary: Greek eleeo (G1653), to shew mercy; hugiaino (G5198), to be sound; Hebrew raah (H7462), to feed, shepherd.
roots_lines: Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound, healthy; 2 Timothy 1:13.
Hebrew raah (H7462) — to feed, tend a flock; Jeremiah 3:15.
Hebrew sakal (H7919) — to understand, act wisely; Jeremiah 3:15.
Greek antilego (G483) — to speak against, gainsay; Titus 1:9.
usage: “but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16) — his answer to the Wesleyans.
“pastors according to mine heart” (Jer 3:15) — the ordinations of 1811.
“Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) — the theologian's task in a revival.

pos: n. (Bridget Bevan, 1698–1779, of Laugharne, patron and manager of Griffith Jones's Welsh circulating schools)
etymology: Irish Brighid, exalted; Welsh Bevan, from ab Evan, son of Evan.
biblical_def: Bridget Bevan, known in Wales simply as Madam Bevan, was the daughter of John Vaughan of Derllys, a Carmarthenshire gentleman who had supported the work of the SPCK, and the wife of Arthur Bevan, member of Parliament for Carmarthen. She became the chief patron, correspondent, and eventually the manager of the circulating schools founded by Griffith Jones of Llanddowror, in which itinerant teachers spent three months in a parish teaching children and adults to read the Welsh Bible and the catechism before moving on. By Jones's death in 1761 the schools had taught well over a hundred thousand people to read, and Madam Bevan carried on the work for eighteen more years from her home at Laugharne, raising money, appointing teachers, and publishing the annual reports. At her death in 1779 she left a large sum to continue the schools, but her will was contested in the Court of Chancery and the money was locked up for a generation; the schools ceased. Wales owed much of its literacy and its Methodist revival to her. She was a woman “full of good works and almsdeeds” (Act 9:36), and her schools obeyed the proverb, “Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a patron as one who countenances, supports and protects a person or a work.
webster_full: PA'TRON, n. One who countenances, supports and protects either a person or a work.
CHAR'ITY, n. Liberality to the poor, consisting in almsgiving or benefactions, or in gratuitous services to relieve them in distress.
LIT'ERATURE, n. Learning; acquaintance with letters or books.
scriptures: Act 9:36
Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas: this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did.
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
She stretcheth out her hand to the poor; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy.
Gal 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
corruption_summary: A Welsh gentlewoman who kept a nation reading the Bible for eighteen years after its founder died.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Madam Bevan is sometimes enlisted as a pioneer of women's leadership. The honest record is better than the slogan: she did not preach or govern the church, but used her wealth, her pen, and her management to serve the ministry of a pastor and the teaching of the poor, as the women of Luk 8:3 ministered to Christ of their substance. The godly woman of Proverbs is the pattern: “She stretcheth out her hand to the poor” (Pro 31:20).

The principle to recover is the endurance of good works. A work begun by one servant is often kept alive by another, and Paul's word is to the second as much as to the first: “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9). The lawsuit that closed her schools is a sober reminder that a bequest is not a substitute for a church that will carry on the work.
roots_summary: Greek ergon (G2041), work; eleemosune (G1654), almsdeeds; Hebrew chanak (H2596), to train.
roots_lines: Hebrew chanak (H2596) — to train up, dedicate; Proverbs 22:6.
Greek ekkakeo (G1573) — to faint, lose heart; Galatians 6:9.
usage: “full of good works and almsdeeds” (Act 9:36) — a Dorcas of Laugharne.
“Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6) — the circulating schools.
“let us not be weary in well doing” (Gal 6:9) — eighteen years after Llanddowror.

pos: n. (the Covenanter bond found on Henry Hall of Haughhead at South Queensferry in June 1680, renouncing Charles II)
etymology: Queensferry, the crossing of the Forth named for Queen Margaret of Scotland; Latin papyrus, paper.
biblical_def: The Queensferry Paper was a draft covenant seized at South Queensferry on 3 June 1680, when government agents tried to arrest Donald Cargill and his companion Henry Hall of Haughhead. Cargill escaped wounded; Hall was mortally injured and died on the way to Edinburgh, and the unsigned paper was found on him. It is generally attributed to Cargill. Its signers bound themselves to the true reformed religion, to the overthrow of the kingdom of darkness, and to the establishment of government according to God's law and the example of the Scriptures; it declared that the king and his ministers, by breaking the Covenants and persecuting the church, had forfeited their right to rule; and it pledged its subscribers to defend themselves and one another against those who sought their lives. Three weeks later Richard Cameron published the Sanquhar Declaration in similar terms. The Paper stands at the hinge of the Covenanter struggle, where field-preachers who had pleaded for liberty began to say openly that a ruler who wars against Christ's church has unmade his own authority. Its question is the psalmist's: “Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?” (Psa 94:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bond as an obligation imposing a duty, and to renounce as to disown or reject.
webster_full: BOND, n. Obligation; an obligation imposing a moral duty, as by a vow or promise.
RENOUNCE', v.t. To disown; to disclaim; to reject; to refuse to own or acknowledge as belonging to.
FORFEIT, v.t. To lose or render confiscable, by some fault, offense or crime.
scriptures: Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?
And Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people, that they should be the LORD'S people; between the king also and the people.
Jer 50:5
They shall ask the way to Zion with their faces thitherward, saying, Come, and let us join ourselves to the LORD in a perpetual covenant that shall not be forgotten.
Act 4:19
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.
corruption_summary: A Covenanter bond that declared a persecuting king had forfeited his throne.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Queensferry Paper is easily dismissed as fanaticism or easily enlisted for revolution. It is neither. Its argument is the Reformed doctrine of the covenanted magistrate, worked out by Knox and Rutherford: that kings rule under God and under covenant, as Jehoiada “made a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people” (2Ki 11:17), and that a ruler who makes war on the church has broken the terms of his office.

The honest caveat is that some of its framers spoke of setting up a commonwealth by their own hands, which no private company of believers has authority to do; the better Covenanter writers kept resistance to lawful defence led by lesser magistrates. The principle to recover is Peter's, which the Paper rests on at its best: “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19).
roots_summary: Hebrew kisse (H3678), throne; chabar (H2266), to have fellowship; berith (H1285), covenant.
roots_lines: Hebrew kisse (H3678) — a throne, seat of honour; Psalm 94:20.
Hebrew chabar (H2266) — to be joined, have fellowship; Psalm 94:20.
usage: “which frameth mischief by a law” (Psa 94:20) — persecution by statute.
“a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people” (2Ki 11:17) — the covenanted throne.
“a perpetual covenant that shall not be forgotten” (Jer 50:5) — what the signers swore to.

pos: n. (the testimony posted at the market cross of Rutherglen on 29 May 1679 by armed Covenanters, three days before Drumclog)
etymology: Rutherglen, a burgh near Glasgow, from Gaelic ruadh, red, and gleann, glen; Latin declaratio.
biblical_def: The Rutherglen Declaration was published on 29 May 1679, the anniversary of Charles II's restoration and his birthday, which the government had appointed as a holy day of thanksgiving. Some eighty armed Covenanters under Robert Hamilton and Thomas Douglas rode into Rutherglen, put out the bonfires lit in the king's honour, publicly burned the acts of Parliament that had overturned the National Covenant and the Solemn League and Covenant, established prelacy, and outlawed field-meetings, and fixed to the market cross a testimony against those acts and against the persecution of the faithful since 1660. They declared that the day of the king's restoration was a day of mourning for the church, since it had brought the overthrow of the covenanted work of reformation. Three days later, on Sunday 1 June, John Graham of Claverhouse attacked a conventicle at Drumclog and was routed, and the rising that ended at Bothwell Bridge began. The Rutherglen men stood where the three young men of Babylon stood when an idol was set up by the king's order: “we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up” (Dan 3:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a testimony as an open attestation or profession, and prelacy as the government of the church by prelates.
webster_full: TES'TIMONY, n. Open attestation; profession. In Scripture, the two tables of the law.
PREL'ACY, n. The office or dignity of a prelate; episcopacy; the order of bishops.
CROSS, n. A market cross, a cross set up where markets are held.
scriptures: Dan 3:18
But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
Have respect unto the covenant: for the dark places of the earth are full of the habitations of cruelty.
And they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul;
Act 4:19
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.
corruption_summary: A public testimony burned onto the king's birthday against the acts that overthrew the Covenants.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The burning of the acts at Rutherglen is the act of men who believed national covenants bind nations, as Judah's did when “they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers” (2Ch 15:12). A king who had sworn the Covenant at his coronation in 1651 and then caused it to be burned by the hangman had, in their view, committed public perjury, and the faithful owed a public testimony against it.

The honest caveat is that the Rutherglen men chose an armed demonstration where a written testimony would have served, and that the rising it provoked ended in slaughter and in sharper persecution. The principle to recover is the duty of public witness against public sin, made in the spirit of the psalmist's prayer, “Have respect unto the covenant” (Psa 74:20), and not in the spirit of party.
roots_summary: Aramaic pelach (H6399), to serve; segid (H5457), to worship; Hebrew darash (H1875), to seek.
roots_lines: Aramaic segid (H5457) — to fall down, worship; Daniel 3:18.
Hebrew nabat (H5027) — to look upon, have respect; Psalm 74:20.
usage: “we will not serve thy gods” (Dan 3:18) — refusal of the king's holy day.
“Have respect unto the covenant” (Psa 74:20) — the prayer behind the testimony.
“to seek the LORD God of their fathers” (2Ch 15:12) — the covenant they would not burn.

pos: n. (the testimony of the United Societies published at Lanark on 12 January 1682 against the Test Act)
etymology: Lanark, a Scottish burgh, from Brittonic llanerch, a clearing; Latin declaratio.
biblical_def: The Lanark Declaration was the first public act of the United Societies, the network of praying societies formed by the Cameronian remnant after the deaths of Richard Cameron at Airds Moss and Donald Cargill on the scaffold. On 12 January 1682 a company of their men entered Lanark, burned the Test Act and the Act of Succession at the market cross, and posted a declaration renewing the testimony of Sanquhar and Rutherglen. The Test Act of 1681 required every officeholder, minister, and schoolmaster to swear an oath that acknowledged the king as supreme governor in all causes, ecclesiastical as well as civil, and that pledged never to seek any change in church or state; the Act of Succession secured the throne to the king's Roman Catholic brother, James, Duke of York. The Lanark men declared that they could neither swear such an oath nor own a papist successor, and that a government which demanded both was making war on the Lord Jesus Christ as King of His church. The Earl of Argyll himself had been condemned for treason that winter for taking the Test only with a qualification. The Declaration rests on Christ's promise to those who will not deny Him: “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father” (Mat 10:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a test as an oath required of officeholders, and supremacy as the highest authority.
webster_full: TEST, n. In England, an oath and declaration against transubstantiation, which all officers must take within six months after their admission.
SUPREM'ACY, n. State of being supreme or in the highest station of power; highest authority or power; as the supremacy of the king of Great Britain.
SUCCES'SION, n. The lineage of the throne; the right of taking possession of a throne.
scriptures: Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven.
Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?
Rev 2:13

I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is: and thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith, even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you, where Satan dwelleth.
Dan 3:18
But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
corruption_summary: A refusal to swear the royal supremacy over Christ's church or to own a papist successor.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the royal supremacy over the church, which the Test Act required men to swear, as a usurpation of Christ's crown rights. The Headship of Christ over His church is the doctrine for which the Covenanters died, and no king, parliament, or modern state may claim to be governor of the church in spiritual causes. The church of Pergamos was commended for the same fidelity in the city of Satan's seat: “thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith” (Rev 2:13).

Modern accounts that treat the Test controversy as a dispute over religious toleration miss its centre. The Test did not ask men to tolerate others; it asked them to swear that the king was head of the church and that nothing must ever change. A state that frames such oaths is the throne Psa 94:20 describes, “which frameth mischief by a law” (Psa 94:20).
roots_summary: Greek homologeo (G3670), to confess; arneomai (G720), to deny; martus (G3144), martyr.
roots_lines: Greek emprosthen (G1715) — before, in the presence of; Matthew 10:32.
usage: “him will I confess also before my Father” (Mat 10:32) — the reward of refusing the Test.
“hast not denied my faith” (Rev 2:13) — the Societies' fidelity.
“nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up” (Dan 3:18) — an oath refused.

pos: n. (the Apologetical Declaration and Admonitory Vindication of the United Societies, posted in November 1684 and drafted chiefly by James Renwick)
etymology: Greek apologia, a speech in defence; Latin declaratio.
biblical_def: The Apologetical Declaration was fixed to market crosses and church doors across south-west Scotland on 8 November 1684 by the United Societies, the remnant of the Cameronian Covenanters, whose field-preacher was the young James Renwick. By that year soldiers and informers were hunting the Societies' people through the moors, and several had been betrayed and killed. The Declaration reaffirmed the Societies' disowning of Charles II's authority, and then added a warning: those who continued to shed their blood, whether as soldiers, judges, or informers, would be regarded as enemies of God and of the covenanted reformation, and might expect to be dealt with as such, though the Societies abhorred the private killing of any man for his opinion. The Privy Council answered within days with the Abjuration Oath, requiring every person to renounce the Declaration on pain of death, and authorized soldiers to put to death on the spot anyone who refused it. The months that followed, through 1685, were the worst of the Killing Time: men shot at their own doors, and two women, Margaret MacLachlan and Margaret Wilson, drowned at the stake in the Solway. The martyrs' cry is the cry of the souls under the altar: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood” (Rev 6:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an apology as a defense or vindication, and abjuration as a renunciation upon oath.
webster_full: APOL'OGY, n. An excuse; something said or written in defense or extenuation of what appears to others wrong, or unjustifiable.
ABJURA'TION, n. The act of abjuring; a renunciation upon oath.
VINDICA'TION, n. The act of vindicating; a defense; justification against denial or censure.
scriptures: Rev 6:10
And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?
Wherefore should the heathen say, Where is their God? let him be known among the heathen in our sight by the revenging of the blood of thy servants which is shed.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
corruption_summary: A persecuted people's warning to their persecutors, answered by an oath enforced at the muzzle.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Declaration is often cited as proof that the Covenanters were terrorists. The record does not bear it. A people already being shot without trial warned that those who hunted them would be treated as enemies in war, while disowning private assassination. The government's reply, summary execution for refusing an oath, is the true measure of who was making war.

The honest caveat is that a warning of reprisal, however provoked, sits uneasily beside the apostle's command, “avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath” (Rom 12:19). The principle to recover is the martyrs' own: “fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul” (Mat 10:28), and leave vengeance to God.
roots_summary: Greek ekdikeo (G1556), to avenge; apokteino (G615), to kill; Hebrew neqamah (H5360), revenging.
usage: “avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth” (Rev 6:10) — the martyrs' appeal.
“the revenging of the blood of thy servants” (Psa 79:10) — vengeance left to God.
“fear not them which kill the body” (Mat 10:28) — the courage of 1685.

pos: n. (David Hackston of Rathillet, d. 1680, Fife laird and Covenanter, taken at Airds Moss and executed at Edinburgh)
biblical_def: David Hackston was a gentleman of Rathillet in Fife who was converted at the field-meetings and joined the persecuted Covenanters. On 3 May 1679 he was present on Magus Muir when a party of Covenanters stopped the coach of James Sharp, archbishop of St Andrews, whom they held responsible for years of persecution, and killed him before his daughter's eyes. Hackston, who had a private lawsuit against Sharp, refused to command the party or to strike a blow lest it be thought revenge, but he did not stop it. He fought at Drumclog and Bothwell Bridge, joined Richard Cameron, and on 22 July 1680 was wounded and taken at Airds Moss, where Cameron was killed. At Edinburgh he was summarily condemned and executed on 30 July with savage cruelty: his hands were cut off, he was hanged and cut down alive, and his heart was torn out. He died professing Christ and the Covenants, with a dying testimony that has been reprinted ever since among the martyrs of the Scots Worthies. He belongs with those who “loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11), and the killing of Sharp stands under Christ's word, “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines assassination as the act of killing by surprise or secret assault, and martyr as one who by his death bears witness to the truth.
webster_full: ASSASSINA'TION, n. The act of killing or murdering, by surprise or secret assault.
MAR'TYR, n. One who, by his death, bears witness to the truth of the gospel.
TES'TIMONY, n. Witness; evidence; proof of some fact; open attestation.
scriptures: And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment:
Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
corruption_summary: A Covenanter martyr whose testimony is honoured and whose part at Magus Muir is mourned.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the killing of Archbishop Sharp as murder, whatever Sharp's guilt. A company of private men stopping a coach on a moor are not a court, and an archbishop's persecution of the church does not transfer the sword from the magistrate to whoever meets him on the road. Christ's rebuke to Peter in Gethsemane governs: “Put up again thy sword into his place” (Mat 26:52).

That judgement does not cancel the rest of Hackston's life. He was condemned without trial, butchered rather than executed, and died confessing Christ. He is among those who “had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment” (Heb 11:36). The principle to recover is that the church may honour the martyr's faith and mourn the man's sin in the same breath.
usage: “they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11) — the scaffold at Edinburgh.
“all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52) — Magus Muir judged.
“slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9) — the Scots Worthies.

pos: n. (John Milne, 1807–1868, minister of St Leonard's, Perth, friend of M'Cheyne and the Bonars, and Free Church minister in Calcutta)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Scots Milne, a mill.
biblical_def: John Milne was one of the circle of young Scottish evangelical ministers who came to maturity in the revival years of the late 1830s with Robert Murray M'Cheyne, Andrew and Horatius Bonar, and William Chalmers Burns. Ordained to St Leonard's, Perth, in 1839, he gave himself to preaching, to house-to-house visitation, and to prayer, and Perth shared in the awakening that spread from Kilsyth and Dundee in those years. At the Disruption of 1843 he came out with his congregation into the Free Church. In 1853 he went to India as minister of the Free Church congregation in Calcutta, where he laboured among Scottish residents and soldiers and supported the mission, returning to Perth in 1857 after the Mutiny. Horatius Bonar wrote his life in 1868, holding him up as a pattern of the affectionate, unwearied pastor. Milne's ministry was the kind Paul described to the Thessalonians: “we were willing to have imparted unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls” (1Th 2:8). His motive was Paul's, “that I might finish my course with joy” (Act 20:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pastor as a minister having the charge of a church and congregation.
webster_full: PAS'TOR, n. A minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation, whose duty is to instruct them in the doctrines of religion and lead them in the practice of evangelical duties.
VISITA'TION, n. The act of visiting; a pastoral visit to members of a congregation.
DISRUP'TION, n. The act of rending asunder; breach; rent.
scriptures: So being affectionately desirous of you, we were willing to have imparted unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls, because ye were dear unto us.

But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.
He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young.
He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.
corruption_summary: A Perth pastor of the M'Cheyne circle whose ministry was visitation, prayer, and plain preaching.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation Milne's life rebukes is the modern reduction of the pastor to manager, communicator, or counsellor. He was a shepherd in the prophet's sense: “He shall feed his flock like a shepherd” (Isa 40:11), and the feeding was by the Word in the pulpit and at the fireside.

The principle to recover is that revival in Scotland came through ordinary means faithfully used: visitation, catechizing, prayer meetings, and preaching. The psalm describes the labour and its fruit: “He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing” (Psa 126:6).
roots_summary: Greek homeiromai (G2442), to be affectionately desirous; dromos (G1408), course; Hebrew raah (H7462), to feed.
roots_lines: Greek homeiromai (G2442) — to long for, be affectionately desirous; 1 Thessalonians 2:8.
usage: “but also our own souls” (1Th 2:8) — the pastor's self-giving.
“finish my course with joy” (Act 20:24) — Perth to Calcutta and back.
“He shall feed his flock like a shepherd” (Isa 40:11) — the pattern of his visitation.

pos: n. (Islay Burns, 1817–1872, successor of M'Cheyne at St Peter's, Dundee, professor at the Free Church College in Glasgow, and biographer of his brother William)
etymology: Gaelic Ile, the island of Islay, used as a Christian name; Scots Burns, a dweller by the stream.
biblical_def: Islay Burns was a son of the manse of Kilsyth and a younger brother of William Chalmers Burns, whose preaching in Kilsyth and Dundee in 1839 had been the means of a remarkable awakening. When Robert Murray M'Cheyne died in March 1843, at twenty-nine, Islay Burns was called to succeed him as minister of St Peter's, Dundee, and a few weeks later led the congregation out at the Disruption into the Free Church. He served St Peter's for over twenty years, keeping a flock shaped by M'Cheyne's ministry in the same plain, searching, Christ-centred preaching. In 1864 the Free Church appointed him professor of church history at its college in Glasgow. His books include a history of the church in the first centuries and, in 1870, a memoir of his brother William, who had died in China in 1868 after twenty years as a missionary there; the memoir did much to make William Burns known as one of the great missionaries of the century. Islay Burns's life was the second generation's calling, to keep and hand on what God had done in the first: “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a memoir as an account of transactions or events written familiarly, and a successor as one who follows another in an office.
webster_full: MEM'OIR, n. A species of history written by a person who had some share in the transactions related; an account of the life of a person.
SUCCES'SOR, n. One that succeeds or follows; one that takes the place which another has left, and sustains the like part or character.
CONGREGA'TION, n. An assembly of persons met for the worship of God, and for religious instruction.
scriptures: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
Jer 3:15
And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding.
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
corruption_summary: M'Cheyne's successor, who kept a revived congregation and wrote his missionary brother's life.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The danger Islay Burns faced is the one every successor to a famous minister faces: to try to be the predecessor, or to try to be his opposite. He did neither, but preached the same gospel in his own voice, as the Lord promised Israel, “pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jer 3:15).

The principle to recover is that the church's memory is a means of grace. His memoir of William Burns did for the next generation what Psa 78:4 commands, “shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4), and sent men to the field who had never heard his brother preach.
roots_summary: Greek agonizomai (G75), to fight, strive; teleo (G5055), to finish; tereo (G5083), to keep.
usage: “I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7) — the successor's fidelity.
“which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jer 3:15) — St Peter's after 1843.
“commit thou to faithful men” (2Ti 2:2) — the Glasgow professorship.
